newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK, Taiwan shipowners seek flag compromise.
newsitem.headline: HK, Taiwan shipowners seek flag compromise.

text.p: The Hong Kong Shipowners' Association hopes to sign an agreement soon on the question of flags flow by Hong Kong and Taiwan ships in each other's ports after China retakes Hong Kong, its spokesman said on Tuesday.
Michael Farlie told Reuters that Taipei and Beijing, which have no official contact, insisted that the issue could not be discussed at government level.
"That is why it has come down to the shipowners' association level," Farlie said. "Any agreement that is signed will be signed between the respective shipowners' associations."
Hong Kong-registered ships will fly the Chinese flag above the future Hong Kong flag after China assumes control over the territory on July 1 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
But uncertainty has surrounded the question of whether Taiwan, which does not recognise China's government, will allow the Chinese-flagged vessels into its ports.
Farlie said Taiwan and Hong Kong shipowners opened discussions in December and he was optimistic a solution was close.
"It doesn't look as if there's the possibility (that) a meeting and a signing will take place until the first week of May," Fairlie said.
Beijing had rejected the suggestion that ships registered in Taiwan and Hong Kong lower their flags when entering each other's waters after July 1, but Farlie said he believed the idea was feasible.
"I think it'll work. The no-flag system is the most pragmatic."
Hong Kong Marine Department Deputy Director Tsui Shung-yiu said the government was not involved in the discussions.
"Hong Kong is an open port," said Tsui. "We welcome every ship that comes to Hong Kong."
Hong Kong has 528 ships registered to the territory, totaling 7.34 million gross registered tons, according to Marine Department figures.
Taiwan and China split in 1949 at the end of a civil war and Beijing still regards Taiwan as a renegade province.

Two Chinese ships sailed directly across the Taiwan Strait this week for the first time in decades under an agreement reached by Beijing and Taipei that allows Chinese ships to process their cargo at a new "offshore transshipment centre" at the southern Taiwan port of Kaohsiung.
